hints: Use the departure-before-admission statement to orient Ramesh relative to Jiten.

questions.solution: Ramesh is senior to Jiten. Since Jiten and Anwar are batchmates between Ramesh and Prakash, the order begins Ramesh, then Jiten=Anwar, then Prakash. questions.theory: An ordering problem is solved by translating each statement into a relation before combining relations. If two people study for the same fixed duration, earlier admission and earlier graduation give the same seniority order. “Between” does not by itself specify which endpoint is earlier; an additional inequality must fix the orientation. A conclusion is necessary only when it holds in every ordering satisfying the premises. To reject a proposed conclusion, construct one compatible ordering in which it fails. For categorical statements, represent classes by sets: “all A are B” means A is a subset of B, whereas “some A are B” asserts a nonempty intersection. Do not infer that a universal inclusion guarantees existence.

questions.prompt: The geometric mean of 100 observations is 25. If each observation is multiplied by 4, what will be the new geometric mean?
hints: Write the original mean as the hundredth root of a product.

questions.theory: For positive observations x_1,...,x_n, the geometric mean is G=(x_1...x_n)^(1/n). Equivalently, log G is the arithmetic mean of their logarithms. Multiplying every observation by a positive constant c multiplies the product by c^n and the geometric mean by c. This homogeneity differs from multiplying the product alone by c, which would multiply the mean by c^(1/n). Geometric means naturally summarize multiplicative growth and ratios; zero or negative observations require separate conventions and generally cannot be handled by the real logarithmic definition. For equal weights all observations contribute equally. A useful check is that a mean of equal observations must equal that common observation, and any scaling formula should preserve this property.

questions.theory: In mixture problems, convert a component ratio into a fraction of the whole before adding quantities. hints: Both bars approach the same surrounding temperature.
Their temperature difference decays with time without changing sign.
questions.solution: For T_i(t)=T_s+(T_i(0)-T_s)e^(-kt), T_1-T_2=(T_1(0)-T_2(0))e^(-kt). The curves never cross and approach the same limiting temperature, as in figure C. Figures A and D cross; figure B shows separated limiting levels. Thus option C is correct.
questions.theory: Newton’s law of cooling models a body in fixed surroundings by dT/dt=-k(T-T_s), where k>0 and T_s is the surrounding temperature. Its solution is T(t)=T_s+(T(0)-T_s)e^(-kt). Identical bars under the same heat-transfer conditions have the same k and the same limiting temperature T_s. Their temperature difference is their initial difference multiplied by e^(-kt), so its sign cannot change and its magnitude tends to zero. A graph showing crossing or different final temperatures is inconsistent with this model. The hotter bar initially cools faster in absolute degrees per unit time. This model assumes approximately uniform internal temperature and a constant heat-transfer coefficient; those assumptions underlie the qualitative exam diagram.

questions.theory: Periodic events occurring at integer intervals coincide again after the least common multiple of the intervals. Once the interval is found, convert seconds into minutes and seconds before adding it to a clock time. For example, an interval of 90 seconds is one minute thirty seconds. For events with different phases, a system of congruences replaces the simple least-common-multiple calculation, and compatibility conditions can prevent any coincidence.

If underlying variables are independent, covariance of two linear combinations is the sum of the products of their corresponding coefficients and variances. A nonzero numerator mean, nonzero denominator mean, or dependence generally changes the ratio law. Dividing by an absolute value also changes the construction unless symmetry restores the same distribution. The denominator equals zero with probability zero for a nondegenerate normal variable.

questions.theory: For a functional integral L(x,y,y′) dx with fixed endpoint values, a sufficiently smooth extremal satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation d/dx(L_(y′))−L_y=0. questions.theory: When subtracting two nearby square roots, rationalize with the conjugate. The identity sqrt(A)−sqrt(B)=(A−B)/(sqrt(A)+sqrt(B)) avoids the indeterminate cancellation of two large terms. For large positive x, divide a denominator involving sqrt(x²+c) by x to obtain sqrt(1+c/x²), which tends to 1. For negative x one must use |x|, since sqrt(x²)=|x|; ignoring this can reverse the sign of a limit. Continuity of the square-root function on positive arguments then completes the calculation. A difference of two quantities tending to infinity need not tend to infinity: their leading growth can cancel. This method often gives a finite limit directly without L’Hôpital’s rule or an asymptotic expansion.

questions.theory: The first-order transport equation u_t+c u_x=0 has characteristic lines x−ct=constant. Along each characteristic u is constant. On a half-line with c>0, tracing a point backward reaches either the initial line t=0 or the inflow boundary x=0. Thus initial data determine the region x>ct and boundary data determine x<ct. The formulas must agree at the characteristic emerging from the corner; matching values gives continuity and matching compatible first derivatives gives a classical C¹ solution. Boundary data cannot be arbitrarily imposed at an outflow boundary. A common error is to use the initial-data formula after the characteristic has entered from the boundary. Check the relevant region before substituting a fixed spatial coordinate.

questions.prompt: For α,β>0 consider Σ_(n≥4)1/[n(log_e n)^α(log_e(log_e n))^β]. Which statement is true?

options.C: It converges for α=1 and all β∈(1,∞).

questions.solution: The corresponding integral becomes∫dt/[t^α(log t)^β]. For α=1 it becomes∫s^(−β)ds and converges exactly forβ>1, proving C. For α<1 it diverges for every fixedβ, refuting A; α=β=1 gives∫ds/s, refuting B. The same cases refute D. For completeness, α>1 gives convergence for anyβ>0 by comparison with a power t^(−γ),1<γ<α.
questions.theory: For positive eventually decreasing terms, the integral test equates convergence of a series with convergence of its corresponding improper integral. The series 1/[n(log n)^alpha(log log n)^beta] has its threshold at alpha=1. With t=log x, the integral becomes integral dt/[t^alpha(log t)^beta]. For alpha>1 it converges for any fixed beta; for alpha<1 it diverges because logarithms cannot overcome a nonintegrable power. At alpha=1, setting s=log t reduces it to integral s^(−beta) ds, convergent exactly when beta>1. A finite number of starting terms does not affect convergence. Repeated-log factors matter only at the borderline exponent; treating every logarithm as if it were an ordinary power of n gives the wrong threshold.
